cards.front: Name the three layers of the evaluation pyramid, from base to top.
cards.back: Deterministic checks such as schema and tool-contract tests, then scenario and trajectory evals, then end-to-end judgements by humans or a model judge.

cards.front: The base of the evaluation pyramid runs on every ____, while the top runs on release candidates.
cards.back: Commit. Base checks are cheap and exact, so they run constantly, while expensive judgements run less often.

cards.front: A nightly judged eval keeps failing because the agent sends dates as 12/03 instead of ISO 8601. What should you change?
cards.back: Push the test down the pyramid. Add a base-layer schema check on the tool's date argument, so the failure is caught on every commit in seconds rather than overnight.

cards.front: A team spends 80 per cent of its eval effort on manual review of full conversations. What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
cards.back: Reviews are slow, so regressions slip in between them and releases wait. Shift effort to cheap base checks and replayed scenarios, keeping a small judged and human sample at the top.

cards.front: Where should golden-set cases come from?
cards.back: From real traffic and incidents. Every incident or wrong answer becomes a regression case, labelled against the written rubric.

cards.front: Keep a ____ split of the golden set that prompt tuning never touches.
cards.back: Held-out. Its score shows whether a change generalises or has only been tuned to the visible cases.

cards.front: Refunds are 5 per cent of traffic. Why does a 400-case random sample give a poor refund score, and what is the fix?
cards.back: It holds only about 20 refund cases, so the per-type score is noisy. Stratify by task type and difficulty so each type, including refunds, has enough cases.

cards.front: A refund score is 90 per cent on 100 cases. Roughly how precise is it, and how would 20 cases compare?
cards.back: The standard error is about 3 points at 100 cases. With 20 cases it rises to nearly 7 points, too wide to detect most regressions.

cards.front: Name four requirements for a trustworthy LLM judge.
cards.back: A written rubric, quoted evidence from the output for each score, structured output, and measured agreement with human labels.

cards.front: Never grade an answer with the same ____ that produced it.
cards.back: Prompt. A judge that shares the producer's prompt shares its blind spots and tends to approve its own reasoning.

cards.front: On 200 human-labelled answers, a 1 to 5 judge matches exactly on 124 and is within one point on 182. Report its agreement.
cards.back: Exact agreement is 62 per cent and within-one accuracy is 91 per cent. State both, with the rubric version and judge model they apply to.

cards.front: Name three judge biases and one control for each.
cards.back: Position bias: run pairwise comparisons in both orders. Verbosity bias: make the rubric penalise unsupported length. Self-preference bias: use a judge from a different model family.

cards.front: Name the levels of an agent's span hierarchy.
cards.back: The run span, then one step span per loop turn, then the model call, tool call, retrieval and guard spans inside each step.

cards.front: OpenTelemetry GenAI ____ conventions make agent traces portable between tools.
cards.back: Semantic. Standard attribute names for the model, tokens and operation mean any compatible backend can read the trace.

cards.front: An llm.answer span records 2,100 input and 420 output tokens. At $2 and $10 per million respectively, what is its cost?
cards.back: $0.0042 for input plus $0.0042 for output, so $0.0084. Store it as the span's cost attribute, so run cost is a simple sum.

cards.front: Where does trace debugging start, and where does it stop?
cards.back: It starts at the symptom and walks backwards through earlier spans. It stops at the first span whose status or attributes are anomalous.

cards.front: A run's costliest span is a large-model fallback answer. Four slow tool.get_order spans come before it. Which span do you inspect first, and why?
cards.back: The first slow tool.get_order. The retries and the costly fallback both follow from that timeout, so fixing the answer call would treat a consequence.

cards.front: A guard.injection span has status ok, but the agent then closed an account nobody asked to close. What do you check?
cards.back: Compare its attributes with a healthy run. If it scanned only 2,000 characters of a 6,400-character document, an instruction later in the text was never seen. Status ok reflects only what the guard saw.

cards.front: List the four release stages in order.
cards.back: Offline eval, shadow, canary, full rollout.

cards.front: Safety assertion failures block ____; quality regressions block only when statistically significant.
cards.back: Absolutely. One safety failure stops the release whatever the average quality score says.

cards.front: On 300 items, a new prompt wins 41, loses 29 and ties 230. Is the gain significant by a sign test?
cards.back: No. Only the 70 non-ties count. Wins would average 35 with a standard deviation near 4.2, and 41 is about 1.4 deviations above, short of the usual 2.

cards.front: A prompt raises judged quality 2 points and cost per conversation from $0.02 to $0.06. At 200,000 conversations a month, how do you present it?
cards.back: Show both: the gain, and monthly spend rising from $4,000 to $12,000, or $8,000 more. Shipping it is then an explicit business trade, not a hidden side effect.
